note: A way of telling the time by geography. When it is noon about six thousand miles to the east, it is roughly an hour before sunrise where the watcher stands. The whole opening describes dawn putting out the stars.
The earth's shadow is the night. It points away from the sun, so as the sun nears the horizon the cone of shadow sinks until it lies almost level.

quote: the radiant servant of the sun
note: Aurora, the dawn, who goes ahead of the sun as his handmaid.
The nine rings of angels Dante has been watching since Paradiso 28, wheeling around a single point of light. They fade from his sight as stars fade at daybreak.
God, seen in Paradiso 28 as a point of light too sharp for the eye to bear.

quote: enclosed by what it itself encloses
note: The point looked as if it sat inside the rings of angels. In truth God contains them and everything else.

context: At each new heaven she has grown more beautiful. Here, at the last one, Dante gives up trying to describe her.

note: For Dante these were the two great kinds of poetry: tragedy in the high style, comedy in a plainer one, with a happy ending. He means any poet at all, and he calls his own poem a comedy.

quote: the first day I saw her face
note: They met as children in Florence, when Dante was nine, as he tells in his early book, the Vita Nuova. He has been writing about her ever since.
His poetry. The poem is close to its end, and he leaves Beatrice's beauty to be praised by something greater than verse.

context: They have just risen out of it, and so out of the physical universe altogether.

quote: the heaven that is pure light
context: The true home of God, the angels and the blessed. The souls Dante met in the spheres below only came down to greet him: they all live here.

note: A famous three lines, built as a chain: light, then love, then joy, each growing out of the one before. The light is intellectual because it is seen by the mind, not the eye. To know God is to love him, and to love him is joy.
The angels, and the human souls who have been saved.

The saved will get their bodies back at the Last Judgment, at the end of time. By a special favor Dante sees them already as they will look then, with human faces, where until now he has seen only lights.
Medieval science held that sight worked through fine "spirits" running between the eye and the brain. Too strong a light scattered them and left the eye blind for a while.

quote: a living light flashed around me
note: Dante's wording echoes the blinding of Saint Paul on the road to Damascus, when "a great light shone round about me" (Acts 22). Paul too was struck blind so that he could see anew.

quote: to prepare the candle for its flame
note: The soul is the candle and the sight of God is the flame. The blinding flash makes the newcomer ready to be lit.
Theologians taught that no created mind can see God by its own strength. God must first raise its power of sight with a gift they called the light of glory. This is that gift.
The image recalls the "river of water of life, bright as crystal" that flows from God's throne in the last chapter of the Bible (Revelation 22).

context: The sparks will turn out to be angels and the flowers the souls of the blessed. The angels pass back and forth between God's light and the souls.

note: Dante calls them topazes, a golden-yellow stone. A few lines earlier the same sparks were rubies.
The river, sparks and flowers are not illusions. They are a first sketch of the real thing, as much as Dante's eyes can take so far. In Italian the phrase is "umbriferi prefazi".

quote: to make better mirrors of my eyes
note: He bathes his eyes in the river of light so that they can take in and reflect more of it. He drinks with his eyelids, not his mouth: in this heaven, to see is to be fed.

quote: from its length into a perfect circle
note: The river becomes a round lake of light. A line has a beginning and an end, like time. A circle has neither, and is the old figure of eternity and of God.
The sparks are now seen as angels and the flowers as the blessed souls. The image changes from a riverbank to a court, and then to a vast flower.
In the Italian, the word "vidi", I saw, ends three lines in this passage, rhyming only with itself. Dante does this with very few words in the poem, among them the name of Christ.
The light of glory, by which angels and souls see God. It lies as a great round lake at the center of everything Dante now sees.

quote: the summit of the Prime Mover
note: A ray from God strikes the top of the Primum Mobile, the outermost turning sphere, and spreads out there as this lake of light. The same ray gives that sphere its motion, which it hands down to all the heavens below.
The blessed sit in rising rings around the lake of light, like the banks of an amphitheater, and are mirrored in it as a hill is mirrored in water.

context: Named here for the first time. The lake of light at its center is already far wider than the sun, and the petals spread outward from there.

quote: near and far neither add nor subtract
note: The Empyrean is outside space, so distance does not blur anything. Dante sees the farthest face as clearly as the nearest.
The yellow heart of the rose is the lake of light. Beatrice leads Dante into the middle of it, with the petals rising all around.
The saved in the Bible's last book stand before God's throne "clothed with white robes" (Revelation 7).
Heaven as the true city, the heavenly Jerusalem. Beatrice, like Dante, was a citizen of Florence, a city he will soon set against this one (Canto 31).
Heaven has a fixed number of seats and most are taken. Dante believed, as many did in his day, that the world was in its last age and the end not far off.
An empty seat with a crown lying on it, waiting for its owner. It is the one seat in the Rose that Dante singles out as kept for someone still alive in 1300, and he gives it to an emperor.
Heaven, pictured in the Bible as the wedding supper of the Lamb, that is, of Christ (Revelation 19). Henry will die in 1313, eight years before Dante.

context: The journey is set in 1300, so his coming is still in the future. By the time Dante wrote these lines Henry was dead and his cause lost.

note: Henry entered Italy in 1310 to restore peace and imperial rule. Florence and other cities shut their gates against him, and he died in 1313 with nothing settled.
Addressed to the Italians. For Dante greed is the root of the world's disorder, the she-wolf of Inferno 1. Italy refuses the one ruler who could feed her, like a hungry child pushing away the breast.

context: He invited Henry into Italy and publicly backed him, then worked against him once he had arrived.

quote: God will not long endure him
note: Clement died in April 1314, eight months after Henry.

context: In Inferno 19 the popes who sold holy things are stuck head down in holes in the rock, their feet on fire. Each new arrival pushes the one before him deeper in.
Alagna is Anagni, the town where he was born. Clement will drop into the hole on top of him. These harsh words are the last Beatrice speaks in the poem.
